question: You run `g = sns.displot(air_quality, x='TEMP')`. Which call relabels its axes?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: `set_xlabel()` is a method of a Matplotlib `Axes`, which is what `histplot()` returns, not `displot()`.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: Correct. `displot()` is figure-level and returns a `FacetGrid`, whose `set_axis_labels()` sets both labels.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Labels are set on the returned object, not passed as a function argument.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: That renames DataFrame columns; `g` is a `FacetGrid`, not a DataFrame.

hints: Work out whether `displot()` is figure-level or axes-level.

question: Which statement about Seaborn's `histplot()` is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It returns a `FacetGrid` that manages the whole figure
options.Explanation: That is what figure-level functions such as `displot()` return.

options.label: B
options.text: It can only draw a KDE curve
options.Explanation: `histplot()` draws a histogram; a KDE is `displot(kind='kde')`.

options.label: C
options.text: It returns a Matplotlib `Axes`, so labels are set with `ax.set_xlabel()`
options.Explanation: Correct. Axes-level functions draw onto one `Axes` and return it.

options.label: D
options.text: It needs `kind='hist'` or it draws nothing
options.Explanation: `histplot()` always draws a histogram; `kind` belongs to the figure-level `displot()`.

hints: Think about what an axes-level function returns.

question: You want the proportion of hours with temperature at or below each value. Which call fits?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A KDE shows a smooth density curve, not a cumulative proportion.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A count plot counts categories; temperature is a continuous number.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: That is a scatter plot of two numerical features.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Correct. An ECDF plots, for each value, the proportion of points at or below it.

hints: Look for the cumulative view of a distribution.

question: `sns.displot(air_quality, x='TEMP', height=3, aspect=2)` produces a figure of what width?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: Correct. Width = `aspect` × `height` = 2 × 3.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: That is the height; with `aspect=2` the width is twice that.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: That divides height by aspect; width multiplies them.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: That is the `aspect` ratio itself, not the width.

hints: Width is not passed directly; it is derived.

question: A classmate writes `sns.displot(df, x='TEMP', width=8)`. What is wrong?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: Units are not the issue; the parameter does not exist.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no `width` parameter; size is set with `height` and `aspect`
options.Explanation: Correct. The lecture stresses there is no `width`; width = `aspect` × `height`.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: No `kind` adds a `width` parameter.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: `set_theme()` sets the style, such as `whitegrid`, not the figure size.

hints: Check which size parameters Seaborn figure-level functions accept.

question: Which call gives every subsequent Seaborn plot a white background with grid lines?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: `color` changes the colour of the marks in one plot, not the background style.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: `ticks` is a different style without the white grid.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Correct. `set_theme()` sets the theme for all later plots, and `whitegrid` is the white background with a grid.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: `whitegrid` is a style, not a plot kind.

hints: Look for the function that changes the global look.

question: You have two numerical features, `TEMP` and `PRES`, and want to see how they relate point by point. Which plot is the most suitable?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A count plot counts the categories of one categorical feature.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A box plot summarises one numerical feature's distribution, not a relationship.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Sunburst charts show hierarchical part-to-whole data.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Correct. Two numerical features are shown as a scatter plot, one point per row.

hints: Each row should become one mark positioned by both values.

question: How do you colour the points of `sns.relplot(data=air_quality, x='TEMP', y='PRES', kind='scatter')` by quarter?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: Correct. `hue` maps a categorical feature to point colour.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: `color` sets one fixed colour for all marks; it does not map a feature.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: `col` splits the figure into one sub-plot per quarter rather than colouring points.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: `size` maps a feature to marker size, not colour.

hints: Seaborn has a parameter that maps a feature to colour.

question: A box plot of PM2.5 by temperature category shows which statistics for each category?

options.label: A
options.text: The mean with a confidence interval
options.Explanation: That is what a bar or point plot shows.

options.label: B
options.text: The minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum, with outliers as separate points
options.Explanation: Correct. A box plot shows those key statistics and the outliers.

options.label: C
options.text: Every individual data point without overlap
options.Explanation: That describes a swarm plot.

options.label: D
options.text: The count of rows in each category
options.Explanation: That is a count plot.

hints: Recall the five numbers a box and its whiskers mark.

question: You want every sepal length for each iris variety shown as its own dot, with no dots overlapping. Which `catplot()` kind fits?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A strip plot shows every point but lets them overlap.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A box plot summarises the distribution rather than showing every point.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Correct. A swarm plot positions individual points so they do not overlap.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: A bar plot shows one estimate per category, not individual points.

hints: Two kinds show every point; only one avoids overlap.

question: If you call `sns.catplot(data=df, x='PM2.5', y='PM2.5_cat')` without a `kind`, what is drawn?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A box plot requires `kind='box'`.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A bar plot requires `kind='bar'`.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: A count plot requires `kind='count'`.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Correct. `'strip'` is the default `kind` of `catplot()`.

hints: Every `kind` parameter has a default.

question: Compared with a box plot, what does a violin plot add for each category?

options.label: A
options.text: The shape of the distribution, drawn as a curve
options.Explanation: Correct. A violin plot shows the distribution curve of each category.

options.label: B
options.text: The count of rows per category
options.Explanation: Counts belong to a count plot.

options.label: C
options.text: A confidence interval around the mean
options.Explanation: That is shown by bar and point plots.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Sub-plots come from `col` or `row`, not from the plot kind.

hints: Think about the shape of the data.

question: Which plot shows extra boxes at further percentiles such as 95%, giving more detail about the tails than a box plot?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A strip plot shows raw points, not percentile boxes.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A KDE plot draws a smooth density curve.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Correct. A boxen plot draws boxes for more percentiles, and `k_depth` controls how many.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: A count plot shows category counts.

hints: Its name sounds like a box plot.

question: What does `sns.relplot(data=air_quality, x='quarter', y='RAIN', kind='line', estimator=sum)` plot for each quarter?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: The mean is the default, but `estimator=sum` replaces it.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: Correct. With `kind='line'` each category gets one y value, and `estimator=sum` makes it the sum.

options.label: C
options.text: Every hourly rainfall value as a dot
options.Explanation: That would be a scatter or strip plot, not a line with an estimator.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Counting rows is a count plot; this sums the `RAIN` values.

hints: `estimator` replaces the default summary statistic.

question: Which call draws one histogram of PM2.5 per quarter, arranged two sub-plots per row?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: `hue` overlays the quarters in one plot by colour; `aspect` only changes the shape.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: `row` stacks the sub-plots one per row, not two per row.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: A pairplot draws pair-wise scatter plots of numerical features.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: Correct. `col` makes one sub-plot per quarter and `col_wrap=2` wraps them two per row.

hints: Sub-plots come from a facet parameter, and another limits how many fit on a row.

question: You want to see a scatter plot of `petal.width` against `petal.length` together with each feature's own distribution along the edges. Which function fits?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: Correct. A joint plot shows the relationship between two numerical features plus their marginal distributions.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: A heatmap shows a matrix of values such as correlations.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: A pairplot shows scatter plots for every pair of features, not one pair with marginals.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: A violin plot shows a numerical distribution per category.

hints: The edge plots are called marginal distributions.

question: In the air-quality correlation matrix, `TEMP` and `PRES` have a correlation of −0.82. What does a heatmap of this matrix make easy to see?

options.label: A
options.text: That temperature and pressure are unrelated
options.Explanation: A coefficient near 0 would mean no linear relationship; −0.82 is strong.

options.label: B
options.text: That higher temperature causes higher pressure
options.Explanation: The sign is negative, and correlation does not show causation.

options.label: C
options.text: A strong inverse relationship: higher temperature goes with lower pressure
options.Explanation: Correct. The lecture notes that strong correlations are easier to find by visualization, such as `sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True))`.

options.label: D
options.text: That pressure has many missing values
options.Explanation: A correlation coefficient says nothing about missing values.

hints: A negative coefficient close to −1 has a meaning.

question: Which call shows how the counts of `PM2.5_cat` differ across temperature categories in a single chart?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: A line plot needs a numerical y to summarise; both features here are categorical.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: Correct. Two categorical features go one on `x` and the other in `hue`.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: Correlations are computed only between numerical features.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: A joint plot is for two numerical features.

hints: Two categorical features: one on the axis, one as colour.

question: Why does the lecture recommend `plotly.express` over building figures with `plotly.graph_objects` alone?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: Every Plotly Express function returns a `plotly.graph_objects.Figure`.

options.label: B
options.text: Graph objects cannot make interactive charts
options.Explanation: Plotly Express uses graph objects internally, so graph objects can make the same figures.

options.label: C
options.text: Plotly Express is a separate package that must be installed on its own
options.Explanation: Plotly Express is a built-in part of the `plotly` library.

options.label: D
options.text: The same figure can take 5 to 100 times more code with graph objects
options.Explanation: Correct. Plotly Express makes a whole figure in one function call.

hints: Compare the amount of code each needs.

question: In `px.scatter(data, x='gdpPercap', y='lifeExp', size='pop', color='continent', hover_name='country', animation_frame='year')`, what does `animation_frame` do?

options.label: A
options.text: It plays the chart as an animation with one frame per year
options.Explanation: Correct. `animation_frame` makes an animated plot over the values of the given feature.

options.label: B
options.text: It sets marker size by year
options.Explanation: Marker size is set by `size`, here population.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows the year when hovering over a point
options.Explanation: Hover labels come from `hover_name` or `hover_data`.

options.label: D
options.text: It draws one sub-plot per year side by side
options.Explanation: That would be faceting; an animation shows the years one after another.

hints: Think about what changes from one frame to the next.
